speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Today's businesses compete with and differentiate themselves from their competitors through innovation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Those who innovate and make good use of their IA and IP have prospered and grown.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Today, IA accounts for more than half of the global value of assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is significant, as it means that intangible assets are worth more than physical assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In other words, ideas and innovations are more valuable than the physical assets that they animate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is to strengthen Singapore's position as a global IA and IP hub, attract and grow innovative enterprises using IA and IP, and develop good jobs and valuable skills in IA and IP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As our businesses generate more IA and IP, the IP registration operations of our IP office become increasingly important.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: An efficient and business-friendly IP office makes it easier for our companies to protect their IA and IP and enhance their value propositions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Singapore has been consistently recognised for our IP regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The World Economic Forum ranks us first in Asia and second globally for IP protection.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) is constantly striving to improve its services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Last year, it was recognised as the third most innovative IP office in the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In our region, over 80% of all requests under the ASEAN Patent Examination Cooperation programme relied on IPOS reports, which is to say, applicants rely on the speed and quality of our patent examination work to speed up their corresponding applications in other ASEAN countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: But the world does not stand still and neither can we.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: IPOS regularly reviews its operations and processes to be more efficient and more importantly, to be business friendly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This Bill is the result and product of such a review.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And based on the responses we have received to our public consultation exercises; our stakeholders are generally supportive of the changes we have tabled today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These changes will result in improvements across three broad categories: first, to ensure enhanced business-friendliness; second, on operational efficiency; and third, to enhance legislative and procedural clarity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To improve IPOS' business-friendliness, the Bill introduces four major changes to improve the experience for applicants seeking to register their IP with IPOS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The first change will streamline the administrative process for international patent applications which are not in English.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Patents Act currently ties certain rights of a patent-holder to the date when the patent application is published, for instance, when determining damages for infringement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, for the 15% or so of the international patent applications that enter Singapore which are not in English, these rights are only conferred if IPOS publishes the English translation of the applications upon the payment of a fee.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 15 removes the requirement for a fee.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Instead, as part of its routine process, IPOS will see to the publication of the English translation received from the applicant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will reduce time, effort and cost for applicants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, we will permit partial acceptance for national trade mark applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is already a common practice in other major jurisdictions, and IPOS already has this practice for international trade mark applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, for national trademark applications, applicants may apply to protect a trademark across multiple types of goods and services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If a trademark examiner has objections to the application in respect of only some of the goods or services listed by the applicant, these objections might hold up the entire application.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: That is approximately 2,100 applications annually, saving applicants time, effort and costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, clause 51(b) changes the post-deadline relief measure for trademark applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under the Trade Marks Act and Rules, trademark applications are treated as withdrawn if certain deadlines are missed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the six months after the deadline, applicants can request reinstatement of their applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This six-month window affects third parties who wish to apply for marks that are identical or similar to the applicant's, as they need to wait for the six-month period to lapse to have greater clarity about the outcome of their own application.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And so, in that period, face uncertainty as to how to proceed in the meantime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To address this situation, applicants will henceforth have two months to request for the continued processing of their lapsed applications, instead of six months to request for reinstatement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Continued processing preserves the application and should the applicant wish to continue with his application, expedites the processing of the application compared to the current approach of seeking reinstatement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The shortened period after the missed deadline will incentivise applicants to quickly put their application in order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The shortened period will also reduce uncertainty for third parties who wish to apply for identical or similar marks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The US and New Zealand similarly provide for a period of two months for applicants to file such a request.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These changes will not affect the majority of applicants who actively monitor applicable deadlines and act in a timely manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The final change in this category introduces an opposition mechanism to facilitate the correction of errors in IP applications or registrations, where the correction may affect the interests of third parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This change pertains to the Geographical Indications Act 2014, the Plant Varieties Protection Act, the Registered Designs Act and the Trade Marks Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Examples of corrections that can affect third parties include those relating to the particulars of the applicant or rights-holder, or that affect the priority details of an application or registration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: IPOS receives about 40 such requests for corrections per year on average.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Resolving such disputes between the applicant or rights-holder and third parties before accepting the corrections enhances the certainty of the information on the Registers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, Members will recall I mentioned changes across three broad categories.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The second category of changes seeks to improve operational efficiency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To begin with, we will improve the patent examination process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, if a patent examiner assesses that a patent application does not satisfy one or more of the requirements to be eligible for the grant of a patent, he or she must issue a written opinion setting out the objections.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will also streamline the patent examination review process to remove unnecessary work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, once a patent examiner has issued a report objecting to the grant of a patent, the applicant can request that the examiner's report be reviewed by filing written submissions and/or amendments to overcome the objections.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Another examiner will then review both the original report and the applicant's responses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, if the applicant files amendments to overcome all unresolved objections mentioned in the original report, that report is no longer relevant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 11 of the Bill therefore changes this so that if the applicant files such amendments, the original report need not be reviewed, and the reviewing examiner can then focus on the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, clauses 22 and 23 introduce a new cooperative mode of examination for applications for the protection of new plant varieties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, during the course of examination, IPOS may appoint external experts to conduct the relevant tests and examination or rely on existing examination reports issued by foreign examiners from approved countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants, of which Singapore is a party, also allows for examiners to rely on relevant tests conducted and submitted by the breeder or another person, organisation or entity acceptable to IPOS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will therefore introduce this option to provide applicants with more flexibility and to reduce turnaround and processing time for such applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The last change in this category lays the groundwork for future improvements to operational efficiency by shifting technical and operational provisions from primary to subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such provisions are common throughout several of our IP statutes, for example, the Plant Varieties Protection Act goes into detail on related information that IPOS must regularly publish, while the Patents Act goes into detail on the amount of time a patent grantee has to renew their patent after expiry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Moving such technical and operational provisions to subsidiary legislation will allow IPOS to adjust and adapt to changing needs more quickly, more nimbly, since amendments to subsidiary legislation can be made more speedily.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The third broad category of changes that the Bill seeks to introduce are those that seek to clarify the law and to smoothen IPOS' administration of the IP prosecution process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are three such changes in the Bill today and let me take Members through.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, clause 17 of the Bill seeks to improve the public's access to patent documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: IPOS had launched the Patents Open Dossier in 2017 to provide easier access to a wider range of patent documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This allows other inventors and the public to better understand inventions for which patent protection is sought or had been granted in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The change introduced in clause 17 clarifies IPOS' ability to make such documents available to the public, even in the absence of any request for the documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, clause 7 amends the Patents Act to empower the Registrar to issue practice directions on the manner of the filing of a patent application, in addition to the manner prescribed in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendment in clause 7 would allow the Registrar to issue practice directions setting out the format in which these sequence listings are to be filed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Sequence listings are listings of nucleotide and/or amino acid sequences, which provide additional detail in patent applications, for instance, in biomedical or biotechnological inventions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such detail can be useful for examiners and subsequent searchers alike.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The law currently has no requirement for patent applications to include such sequence listings even when they might be relevant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Imposing this requirement in the rules and practice directions will strengthen the completeness of patent disclosures and make patent searches easier, more thorough, both for patent examiners and for the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, clause 41 will provide clarity on the period that an expired trademark will continue to be regarded as an "earlier trade mark".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Expired trademarks are currently regarded as earlier trademarks for a year after their expiry and also remain eligible for renewal or restoration during this period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Such expired trademarks continue to retain priority, potentially preventing the registration of other similar marks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, trademark proprietors may have more than a year to renew or restore their expired marks in certain circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For instance, when IPOS granted an extension of time as part of its COVID-19 relief measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The law is currently unclear as to whether such marks, which are still eligible for restoration or renewal after a year, will still continue to be regarded as "earlier trade marks".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will ensure that trademark proprietors who are entitled to renew or restore their marks continue to enjoy the benefits of their registrations against later applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This change will bring IPOS'. management of such monies in accordance with the best practices across the rest of the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These reflect the continued and ongoing efforts of MinLaw and IPOS to review, to refresh and update, and improve the IP registration process in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will support our businesses as they move towards the greater use of IA and IP both locally and globally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new cooperative mode of examination for plant variety protection applications, on the other hand, will be implemented later, after IPOS has finalised the procedural details.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure Minister Edwin Tong will be glad to know I have three quick fire points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, can Minister clarify when a Breeder’s test should be submitted when registering a new plant variety?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 18A of the Plant Varieties Protection Act phrases this as a voluntary option for applicants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This could create uncertainty whether or not to expend resources on the test.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is especially relevant as Breeder’s tests may sometimes take several planting seasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, will the Ministry clarify the principles for interpreting a disclaimer under the Registered Designs Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 30A only states that the rights are "restricted accordingly".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This does not appear to consider that disclaimers may also expand the rights of a registered design.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, can a disclaimer as to colour expand the protection to all designs of that type regardless of colour?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I support the Bill, I will offer some additional points for consideration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My remarks pertain to three areas, just like the other Member, but unfortunately for Minister Edwin Tong, I am both more verbose and more detailed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will talk about drawing a distinction, first, between protection afforded to trade marks and geographical indications vis a vis other classes of intellectual property.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, I will talk about the application of information technology and digitalisation to IP processes and third, I will discuss a notion of a unified act for all IP classes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my prior speech on how intellectual property confers monopoly rights on ideas during the debate on the Copyright Act of 2021, I had spoken about the tradeoffs between granting IP protection and innovative activity and concluded that we should be sensitive to inherent tradeoffs between our pursuit of pre-eminence as a global IP hub and sanctioning potential abuse and overreach via rent seeking behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The moral of that argument applies with special force for the case of trade marks along with – to a lesser degree – geographical indications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Legally enforceable trade marks do not generally promote competitive innovative activity, unlike copyrights or patents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They do not generally enrich the public domain, serving as the germ of subsequent research ideas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Their function is largely market oriented to grant its owners a right to preclude others from the use of a particular established brand or symbol.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More fundamentally, trade marks have a tendency to favour the business interests of incumbents against those of new entrants and challengers to the status quo.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The public policy premise for their existence is therefore correspondingly weaker, and we should, in my view, be more guarded in our treatment of trade marks in our corpus of IP law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The amendments in part 5 of the Bill on trade marks should therefore be scrutinised in this light.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The analogy here is how a small transactions tax, financial transactions tax, could throw "sand in the wheels" and discourage excesses from speculative trading in financial markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, I think it is fair to ask whether as a small open economy with a strong interest in promoting indigenous innovative capacity, whether we should be granting IP rights that could be counterproductive to advancing that endeavour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More pointedly, are we approving trade marks on a partial basis?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Excuse me – are we approving trade marks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Are we granting the registrar the right to approve trade marks on a partial basis instead of the existing default of requiring, a full resubmission, which may well be favourable for fostering a less inhibitive innovation climate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, do we wish to make it easier for applicants to quickly secure IP rights that could then be turned around and used toward profiteering.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One only need to look at trade mark trolls worldwide such as Paris Hilton attempting to trade mark "That's hot!", or Donald Trump seeking to trade mark "You're fired!".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thankfully, they were not successful in these applications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While not explicit in the Bill, there are also two aspects of information technology and digitisation that I believe merits some additional comment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the initial public consultation document issued in August last year, IPOS explained that they have begun the deployment of artificial intelligence technologies for IP administration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular and relevant to this Bill, one use of AI was in assessing extension of time requests in response to correspondence from the registrar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, the two-month period for filing notices of opposition to propose corrections for patent applications would now apply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Presumably, this was inspired as Minister Edwin Tong discussed earlier on by the application of AI to ascertain whether such a two-month duration is reasonable, or at least consistent with the historical data with which IPOS has available.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The strength of big data rests on, well, access to data that are genuinely large.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some rules of thumb are data in excess of one terabyte or training data for machine learning that is in the order of millions of observations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I do not have the visibility on the number of IP applications IPOS has in its internal databases, I would venture that these fall far short of typical applications of machine learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A perhaps more pernicious concern is that unsurprisingly, AI technology is only as intelligent as the historical data on which it trains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has led to arguments by some data scientists who point out that callous applications of AI could exacerbate existing societal fault lines and entrench persistent inequalities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the very least, AI prediction should be subject to scrutiny, not just by standards of fairness and transparency, but also whether historical decisions are being fed into the algorithm are actually truly just or optimal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While such data access is surely welcome, I will only note that the existing design of the POD requires that the user know the parameters for a given IP such as the filing date, applicant name or application number.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These are certainly useful for reverse lookups but is nevertheless relatively constrained, especially when engaged in the free form searches one typically performs in exploratory research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such multiple sources could lead to a proliferation of related laws that run the risk of potential conflict or making searches for IP relevant legislation comparatively less user-friendly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The only justification I can think of for not doing so is the need to remain faithful to various international treaties to which we are party.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such consolidation, however, would not only make it easier for IP and legal professionals to reference laws related to IP while also remaining consistent with the ethos and body in the Statute Law Reform Act, which was passed last year in this House.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng asked about a breeder's test and also about the principles that will apply for interpreting a disclaimer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will deal with these two points first and touch on sustainability issue later on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This involves the breeder or another person, organisation or entity acceptable to the Registrar of Plant Varieties in IPOS, or the Examiner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is known as the breeder’s test which Mr Ng referred to a moment ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng asked when a breeder’s test should be done, so that applicants would be clear when it would be necessary for them to expend the time and resources to do the test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whether a candidate plant variety meets the DUS criteria is established at examination.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, the Registrar may either appoint external experts, as I mentioned earlier, as examiners to conduct examination, including the tests for the DUS criteria, or utilise an existing examination report with results on the DUS criteria, issued by a foreign examiner from an approved country.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: IPOS will conduct further consultations with stakeholders on procedural details before implementing the new breeder’s test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The second item for clarification by Mr Ng relates to the new section 30A of the Registered Designs Act (RDA).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This relates to the disclaiming of rights in relation to a specified feature of a design.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng sought clarification on the principles for interpreting a disclaimer under the RDA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: IPOS’ approach to disclaimers under the RDA takes reference from our trade marks regime, and adopts the same intent and understanding as to the effect of disclaimers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When applying for registered design protection, an applicant may identify what they wish to protect by providing a representation and description of their design, and if necessary, by clarifying which parts of that design they are not seeking protection for.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The intent in providing applicants with the option to make disclaimers is so that applicants can specify which features of a design they do not wish to protect.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the protection conferred on a registered design will include the features that have been described and represented, whilst excluding any features that have been disclaimed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, a disclaimer should only reduce the features that are protected under the registered design.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me turn to Mr Ng's third point on Singapore’s IP strategy and how it can support sustainability innovation and contribute to our fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is an existential challenge for us in Singapore as a small island.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We must get creative and pioneer technological and policy solutions for sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Intellectual property (IP) is a useful tool to drive and support innovation, including innovation in clean technologies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What we can do, and have done, is to help accelerate the pace of innovation by facilitating: (a) better support from our IP regime for the development and use of emerging technologies; (b) technology transfer from the public sector to the private sector to expedite the introduction of new innovations to the market; and finally, (c) faster protection to benefit innovators working in fields with short technology life cycles.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In my opening speech, I mentioned the Singapore IP Strategy 2030, or SIPS 2030.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Part of our commitment under SIPS is to support technological advances through policy reviews.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for instance, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned the new rules that were introduced last November as part of the Copyright Act 2021 to clearly permit computational data analysis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Future reviews will continue to take into account emerging clean technologies and, certainly, future reviews on a broader point will also take into account what Assoc Prof Jamus Lim said about AI and machine learning.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these are developments that continue, they evolve and, over time, new changes will mean that we might need new rules.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we are committed to ensuring that our regime, as a whole, given that we are dealing with a high technology, cutting edge space, we will have to continue to evolve to meet these changes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another commitment under SIPS is to increase enterprise access to publicly funded IP, including for innovations that can benefit our healthcare and sustainability efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the sooner and quicker we are able to do this, the more confidence an innovator will have in the system that it will be able to register and protect its inventions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This reduction in the time needed to acquire protection benefits innovation in fields with short product life cycles in particular and facilitates the rapid commercialisation and proliferation of new technologies which may include green technologies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A strong IP system that recognises invention, protects innovation is one that will promote innovation and promote this space.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim spoke about having more competition for the incumbents, but I will venture to suggest that if we had no IP protection or less IP protection, then in fact the space for the incumbents to be in Singapore will be far less ideal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And you will find that incumbents will take their innovations and inventions elsewhere where they can apply for and obtain trade mark protection.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of competition, I would say that competing goods can actually be sold.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Once again, I thank Members who have spoken – both Mr Ng and Prof Jamus – and support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In summary, this Bill is part of our process, our continual process and efforts to ensure that our IP office and our regime and system that we use, and very often it is not just about the laws but about how they are implemented in practice, what is the procedure like, how quick can we do it, how fast is the turnaround time and how efficient can we deal with applications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of this is part of our efforts to ensure an efficient and a business-friendly environment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This in turn helps our companies, innovators and inventors protect their IP and turn their innovations into a competitive edge and advantage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I wish to clarify that, in fact, I feel that there is a distinction between trade marks as a class versus other classes of intellectual property for the purposes of promoting innovations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, here my question is more whether Minister Tong feels that trade marks should be treated somewhat differently, given that it tends to be conferred more for existing incumbents, as opposed to other classes of intellectual property that is often conferred to new entrants?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For trade marks, in particular, the point is a broader one.
